title: Mole Concept and Stoichiometry
tagline: Mole, molar mass, percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulae, and stoichiometry of reactions.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Chemistry registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Chemistry begins with a sensible way to count particles. Atoms and molecules are too small to count individually, so chemists count them by weighing using the mole. The mole links the invisible world of particles to the visible world of grams, and stoichiometry uses that link to predict how much reactant is consumed or product formed in a chemical reaction. This chapter builds from the definition of the mole to empirical and molecular formulae, and then to the simple arithmetic of chemical equations.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Mole and Avogadro constant; molar mass; percentage composition; empirical and molecular formulae; stoichiometry; limiting reagent

learningOutcomes: Define the mole and use the Avogadro constant in simple calculations.
Convert between mass, moles and number of particles for elements and compounds.
Calculate percentage composition from a formula and determine empirical and molecular formulae.
Balance a chemical equation and use it to calculate reactant and product quantities, including the limiting reagent.

blocks.text: The mole is the counting unit of chemistry. One mole of any substance contains the same number of entities, whether those entities are atoms, molecules, ions or formula units. That number is the Avogadro constant, roughly 6.022 x 10^23 per mole. The mole makes it possible to say that one mole of carbon atoms and one mole of water molecules contain the same number of particles even though their masses are very different.

items: The mole links the mass of a substance to the number of particles it contains.
A mole can refer to atoms, molecules, ions or formula units, depending on the substance.
Avogadro constant = number of particles in one mole.

items.text: One mole of carbon atoms contains 6.022 x 10^23 carbon atoms. One mole of water molecules contains 6.022 x 10^23 water molecules. The two samples have the same number of particles but very different masses.
items.note: The mole is about counting, not about mass being the same.

learn.title: Molar mass and converting mass to moles

blocks.text: The molar mass of a substance is the mass of one mole of that substance, expressed in grams per mole. For an element, the molar mass is numerically equal to its atomic mass in atomic mass units. For a compound, the molar mass is the sum of the molar masses of all the atoms in its formula. Once molar mass is known, converting between mass and moles is straightforward: moles = mass / molar mass.

items: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol.
Moles = mass / molar mass; mass = moles x molar mass.
For a compound, add the molar masses of all atoms in the formula.
Always keep track of units; if mass is in grams and molar mass in g/mol, moles come out correctly.

items.text: The molar mass of water, H2O, is about (2 x 1) + 16 = 18 g/mol. The number of moles in 36 g of water is 36 / 18 = 2 mol.
items.note: The same formula, moles = mass / molar mass, works for any substance once its molar mass is known.

learn.title: Percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulae

blocks.text: Percentage composition tells what percentage of a compound's mass comes from each element. It is calculated from the formula by dividing the total mass of one element in one mole of the compound by the molar mass and multiplying by 100. An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms in a compound, while the molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule. The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

items: Percentage composition is based on mass, not on number of atoms.
Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
Molecular formula = n x empirical formula, where n is a whole number.
To find the empirical formula from percentage data, convert percentages to moles and then find the simplest ratio.

items.text: If a compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass, convert each to moles using atomic masses, then simplify the ratio. If the empirical formula is CH2O and the molar mass is 180 g/mol, the molecular formula is (CH2O) x 6 = C6H12O6, because 180 / 30 = 6.
items.note: The empirical formula alone does not give the actual number of atoms; the molar mass is needed for the molecular formula.

blocks.text: Stoichiometry is the calculation of quantities in chemical reactions. Once a chemical equation is balanced, the coefficients tell the mole ratios between reactants and products. Those ratios are used to work out how much of one substance is used or formed from a given amount of another. In real reactions the reactants are rarely present in exact stoichiometric proportions, so one reactant runs out first; that reactant is called the limiting reagent, and it determines how much product can form.

items: A balanced equation gives the mole ratio between reactants and products.
Stoichiometric calculations go from mass to moles, use the mole ratio, then go back to mass if needed.
The limiting reagent is the reactant that is used up first.
The amount of product is controlled by the limiting reagent, not by the other reactants.

items.text: If 2 mol of hydrogen react with 1 mol of oxygen to make water, 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, then 4 mol of hydrogen would need 2 mol of oxygen. If only 1 mol of oxygen is available, oxygen is the limiting reagent.
items.note: Identifying the limiting reagent is a step before calculating the actual amount of product.

keyPoints: One mole contains 6.022 x 10^23 entities; this is the Avogadro constant.
Moles = mass / molar mass; molar mass of a compound is the sum of its atomic masses.
Empirical formula gives the simplest ratio; molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it.
Percentage composition is calculated from the formula using masses, not atom counts.
A balanced chemical equation gives the mole ratios used in stoichiometric calculations.
The limiting reagent is the reactant that runs out first and controls the amount of product.
examFocus: When finding an empirical formula from percentages, convert to moles first, then simplify the ratio.
In stoichiometry, check which reactant is limiting before calculating the product; the question usually gives masses, so convert to moles first.

vocabulary.meaning: The amount of substance containing 6.022 x 10^23 elementary entities.
The number of particles in one mole, about 6.022 x 10^23 per mole.
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
The actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule.
The reactant that is used up first and determines the amount of product.

questions.prompt: One mole of any substance contains:
questions.explanation: By definition, one mole contains the Avogadro number of entities, whether atoms, molecules or ions.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking one mole is one gram or one atom.

questions.prompt: The number of moles in 18 g of water (molar mass 18 g/mol) is:
questions.commonMistake: Confusing mass in grams with moles.

questions.prompt: The empirical formula of a compound is CH2O and its molecular mass is 180. If the empirical formula mass is 30, the molecular formula is:
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to multiply all atoms in the empirical formula by n.

questions.prompt: Define the limiting reagent in a chemical reaction.
questions.answer: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is completely used up first and therefore controls the amount of product that can form.
questions.explanation: A good answer mentions that it limits the product and is consumed first.
questions.commonMistake: Saying it is the reactant present in the smallest mass, without mentioning moles or reaction proportions.

questions.prompt: Why must a chemical equation be balanced before doing stoichiometric calculations?
questions.answer: A balanced equation gives the correct mole ratio between reactants and products; without balancing, the ratio used in the calculation is wrong.
questions.explanation: Stoichiometry depends on mole ratios from the balanced equation.
questions.commonMistake: Saying a balanced equation is only needed for the final answer, not for the ratio.

questions.prompt: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Calculate its empirical formula. If its molar mass is 60 g/mol, determine its molecular formula.
questions.answer: Moles: C = 40.0 / 12 = 3.33; H = 6.7 / 1 = 6.7; O = 53.3 / 16 = 3.33. Ratio C:H:O = 1:2:1, so empirical formula = CH2O. Empirical mass = 30 g/mol. n = 60 / 30 = 2, so molecular formula = C2H4O2.
questions.explanation: Convert percentages to moles, simplify to the simplest ratio, then use molar mass to find the molecular formula.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at the empirical formula when the molecular formula is asked for.
